bookmap.title: Bookmap — order book and trading in real time
bookmap.intro: This view shows only MEASURED data: the actual Binance order book and actually executed trades. Nothing here is calculated or estimated.

sections.p: Each horizontal cell is resting liquidity — limit orders waiting at that price. Bright means a lot. A continuous bright band is a large order sitting there over time, and such bands often act as resistance because price has to work through them.

One column is exactly one pixel wide and covers the configured interval. At one second per column, a 1200-pixel window shows twenty minutes. A grey vertical stripe marks a gap — the tab was in the background and the connection was closed.

The mid price between best bid and best ask. It comes from the order book, not from completed trades, so it usually sits slightly beside the trade dots. At very tight zoom you can see its steps — those are individual ticks.

Executed trades. Area is the traded quantity, colour is the aggressive side: green means buyers lifted the offer, red means sellers hit the bid. The "group trade dots" slider bundles them in time — without it they merge into a band.

When bubbles pile up at a bright band but the mid price does not get through, absorption is happening: someone is taking the pressure without price giving way. If the line then does break through, a fast move often follows because the resistance is gone.
Real forced liquidations from the Binance stream. Unlike the liquidation map, these are not estimates but events that actually happened.
The volume profile of the visible period: how much was traded at which prices, split by buy and sell. Hovering shows quantity and value. The width is adjustable; at zero it disappears.
Traded volume per time slice, green when buyers were more aggressive. The switch from green to red shows a change of initiative — hard to see in the bubbles alone.
The dashed "snapshot reach" line marks how deep the fetched order book goes. Above and below it the picture is incomplete, not empty — orders do exist there, we just cannot see them.

bookmap.caveat: What you see can change in seconds: limit orders can be pulled at any time. A large band is a statement of intent, not a promise — it may vanish as soon as price approaches.

levmap.title: Liquidation map — where positions would be force-closed
levmap.intro: This view is a MODEL, not a measurement. Binance does not publish position data. All that is known is how many contracts are open in total — from that, likely liquidation prices are estimated.

sections.p: For each candle the change in open interest is examined. If it rises, positions were opened — somewhere within that candle's price range, so the increase is spread evenly across it rather than placed at a point. If it falls, positions were closed and the existing stock is thinned proportionally.

Whether an increase was long or short is decided by the candle's aggressive buy volume. If buyers dominate, the increase counts mostly as long. This is an approximation — nobody but the exchange knows the actual split.
The snapshot: long zones to the left, short zones to the right, centre line at the current price. Bar length is the value in dollars, linearly normalised — twice as long means twice as much.

Time to the right, price upward, colour shows zone mass. Candles are drawn on top, and their wicks show exactly the touches that sweep a zone. On the right is the distribution profile of the current state.

Once price has run through a zone it turns grey — retroactively across its whole history. Only what still stands today, and could still trigger, stays coloured. Without this recolouring every zone ever created would glow forever and the map would become unreadable over time.
"All" mixes them weighted. A single tier is a what-if: if everyone used this leverage, the zones would sit here. 100x hugs the price, 10x sits about ten percent away.

The most important number in the legend: what share of the actual open interest is represented in the map at all. Positions opened before the time window are unknown to the model. Below twenty percent a warning appears — the map then shows only a fraction.

The share of the position the exchange requires to remain as collateral. At 100x leverage and a 0.4 percent rate you may only lose 0.6 percent, not one percent — which is why 100x liquidates at minus 0.6 percent. Binance only releases the real values with an API key; 0.004 is BTCUSDT tier 1. For small coins it is more like one to two and a half percent.

Measured against 9,734 recorded real liquidations: the map marks about thirteen percent of the visited price range and catches roughly twenty percent of actual events within it. That is a factor of 1.54 over chance — measurably better than guessing, but four out of five liquidations happen elsewhere.

levmap.caveat: The biggest fiction: every contract has two sides, and the model assumes only one of each pair is leveraged. It also cannot see cross margin or added collateral. Read the map as "where is a lot compared to the surroundings", not as a price target.

oi.title: Open interest — how much capital is committed
oi.intro: Open interest is the total of all open contracts. It does not say whether the market is bullish or bearish — it says how much is on the table at all. Only together with price does it become meaningful.

sections.p: The blue area is open interest, the white line is price. They share the time axis but have separate scales — what matters is direction, not absolute levels.
The bars show how much was added or removed per time slice. Green means build-up, red means unwinding. The stock itself drifts slowly; the change shows when something actually happened.
New long positions are carrying the move. This counts as a solid advance — fresh money is flowing in rather than old positions merely unwinding.
Shorts covering: sellers close their positions and must buy to do so. The rise is driven by compulsion, not conviction — such moves often stall once the covering is done.
New short positions. The decline is being actively traded, not just passively passed through.
Longs unwinding. Often seen at the end of a decline, when the last holders give up.

Both pages use the same data. What appears here as an increase is distributed across prices there and converted into liquidation zones. A strong build-up without price movement means, for the map, that closely spaced zones are forming.
Short windows use five-minute resolution and reach back about 41 hours; longer ones step up to coarser periods automatically. The span actually achieved is shown in the header.

oi.caveat: Open interest is a net figure. If a thousand positions open and nine hundred close, it shows only a hundred — actual turnover is always larger than the curve suggests.

agent.title: Strategies — how the workflow fits together
agent.intro: This area runs trading strategies automatically: on paper first, and only later — after several approvals — for real. The safe path is always the same: build → measure → observe → only then money.

sections.p: Under "New strategy" you will find ready-made templates (LSOB, MACD cloud, Bollinger+RSI and more) — adopting a template is the fastest start. Your own ideas are assembled from building blocks in the strategy editor, or described in plain words to the chat builder; both produce the same kind of rule set, not program code.

sections.h: 2 · Create an instance — always paper first
sections.p: An instance is a strategy with concrete settings: symbols, timeframe, parameters and risk (risk per trade, daily loss limit, minimum reward/risk). Always start in "paper" mode — the engine then trades simulated money, every 15 seconds, on closed candles.

sections.h: 3 · Measure in the lab before you start
sections.p: The backtest checks your settings against the past — with the same engine as paper trading, including fees and slippage. The most important number is the expectancy per trade in R; below roughly 30 trades a result is not reliable.

A setting that only looks good in the period you picked it in is worthless. The multi test therefore splits the period into two halves — optimisation and verification — and runs several symbols. Adopt a change only if it is better in EVERY cell.

After starting, "Setups" shows what the strategy detects and why setups get discarded (zone broken, reward/risk too low …). "Performance" shows the key figures, the setup funnel, and the timeline chart draws what the agent saw and traded on the price chart.

sections.h: 6 · Put the AI agent to work
sections.p: The "Optimise with AI agent" button (on the instances page and in the lab) hands an instance to the AI coach. It reads the performance data, tests counter-hypotheses in backtests and files an improvement suggestion. Suggestions NEVER change anything on their own — you accept or discard them in the lab.

Before live comes shadow mode: the full live path runs, but the order is only logged. Real trading requires three separate approvals — the global switch in settings, the per-instance approval and enough paper trades. Any trading-relevant change revokes the approval again.

The red emergency stop on the instances page halts all instances immediately and can close open positions. While it is active no instance can be started — it is deliberately lifted only in settings, never by a start click.

agent.caveat: Beta: this area is under development and not investment advice. Backtest numbers are not a promise — a result only counts once it holds outside the period it was chosen on. Let a strategy run on paper long enough before even thinking about live.
